```{r}
#| include: false

# Setup: load packages and the four data files
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(lubridate)
library(survival)
library(ggsurvfit)
library(tidycmprsk)

intakes_old  <- read_csv("data/Intakes_2013_to_2025.csv")  |> clean_names()
intakes_new  <- read_csv("data/Intakes_20261114.csv")      |> clean_names()
outcomes_old <- read_csv("data/Outcomes_2013_to_2025.csv") |> clean_names()
outcomes_new <- read_csv("data/Outcomes_20261114.csv")     |> clean_names()

# ---- Look and feel for every chart ----
species_colors <- c(Dog = "#2F6F6A", Cat = "#E08E45")

theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey35", margin = margin(b = 10)),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey90"),
      axis.title = element_text(colour = "grey30"),
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left"
    )
)
```

## Summary

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Question.** Which characteristics of a shelter animal, and which conditions it arrives in, affect how long it stays at the Austin Animal Center? Can we flag the animals most likely to wait longest, or to have a poor outcome, early enough for the shelter to help?

**Data.** More than 160,000 dog and cat stays from October 2013 to May 2025, from the City of Austin Open Data Portal.

**Early findings.** Dogs and cats leave the shelter in different ways. Roughly half of both are adopted, but about one in four dogs is reclaimed by an owner (versus about one in twenty cats), while more than a third of cats are transferred to other organizations (versus about one in five dogs). Arrival condition matters, especially for cats: about 29% of injured cats and 22% of sick cats died or were euthanized, compared with 12% and 11% of dogs, and under 3% of animals that arrived in normal condition.

Dogs are adopted faster at first (22% of dog stays end in adoption within a week, versus 13% of cats), but by day 90 the two are nearly level, at 46% to 47%.

Age and condition shape where animals go as much as how fast: nearly half of dogs over 5 years old are returned to their owners, and most neonatal animals are transferred.

The importance of age and condition changes during a stay: injured and neonatal animals are adopted far more slowly in the first weeks, but among those still waiting after eight weeks the gap narrows or disappears.

**Still to come.** Written findings from the models of death or euthanasia, and a test of whether animals at high risk can be flagged at intake, using the newer data.
:::

<!-- Update this summary once the death and euthanasia models and the risk-flag test are written up. -->

## Why this matters

Shelters have limited kennel space, staff time, and money. Every extra day an animal stays costs resources and can affect its health and behavior. If a shelter can tell at intake which animals are likely to wait longest or have a poor outcome, it can direct foster care, medical treatment, behavior support, and adoption marketing to those animals sooner.

## The data

Austin Animal Center publishes two datasets on the City of Austin Open Data Portal: **intakes** (animals arriving) and **outcomes** (animals leaving). Each exists in two formats. In May 2025 the published format changed, with different columns and a different animal ID format, so the two periods cannot simply be stacked together.

The main analysis uses the **2013 to May 2025** files. The newer files are set aside to test later how well the results hold up on animals the analysis has not seen.

```{r}
#| echo: false

tibble(
  Dataset = c("Intakes (old format)", "Outcomes (old format)",
              "Intakes (new format)", "Outcomes (new format)"),
  Period  = c("Oct 2013 to May 2025", "Oct 2013 to May 2025",
              "May 2025 to Nov 2026", "May 2025 to Nov 2026"),
  Rows    = c(nrow(intakes_old), nrow(outcomes_old),
              nrow(intakes_new), nrow(outcomes_new))
) |>
  knitr::kable(format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

## Preparing the data

Each row in the intake file is one arrival. To measure how long an animal stayed, I matched each arrival to that animal's **next** departure from the outcomes file, then calculated the days in between. The code for each step is available under "Show code."

### Dates and outcomes

The files store dates in different formats, so I converted them all to plain dates. I also lowercased the outcome labels so that, for example, "Adoption" and "adoption" count as the same thing.

```{r}
#| include: false

# Helper: turn dates stored as text, dates, or date-times into plain dates
to_date <- function(x) {
  if (inherits(x, c("Date", "POSIXt"))) {
    as_date(x)
  } else {
    as_date(parse_date_time(x, orders = c("YbdIMSp",
                                          "YmdHMS",
                                          "Ymd",
                                          "mdYIMSp")))
  }
}

intakes_old <- intakes_old |>
  mutate(intake_id = row_number(),
         intake_date = to_date(date_time))

outcomes_old_clean <- outcomes_old |>
  transmute(animal_id,
            outcome_date = to_date(date_time),
            outcome_type)
```

```{r}
# Lowercase outcome labels so "Adoption" and "adoption" count as the same thing
outcomes_all <- outcomes_old_clean |>
  mutate(outcome_type = str_to_lower(outcome_type)) |>
  distinct()
```

### One row per stay

```{r}
# Step 1: pair each intake with its next outcome
matched <- intakes_old |>
  select(intake_id, animal_id, intake_date) |>
  inner_join(outcomes_all, by = "animal_id", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  filter(outcome_date >= intake_date) |>   # keep outcomes on or after arrival
  group_by(intake_id) |>
  slice_min(outcome_date, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>   # earliest one ends the stay
  ungroup() |>
  select(intake_id, outcome_date, outcome_type)

# Step 2: add those outcomes back onto every intake
data_cutoff <- as_date("2025-05-05")   # where the old files end

stays <- intakes_old |>
  left_join(matched, by = "intake_id") |>
  mutate(still_in_shelter = is.na(outcome_date),
         end_date = coalesce(outcome_date, data_cutoff),
         los_days = as.numeric(end_date - intake_date))
```

### Dogs and cats, and grouped outcomes

```{r}
stays_clean <- stays |>
  filter(animal_type %in% c("Dog", "Cat")) |>
  filter(!intake_type %in% c("Euthanasia Request", "Wildlife")) |>
  filter(!(still_in_shelter & los_days > 365)) |>
  mutate(outcome_group = case_when(
    still_in_shelter                                    ~ "Still in shelter",
    is.na(outcome_type)                                 ~ "Unknown outcome",
    outcome_type == "adoption"                          ~ "Adopted",
    outcome_type %in% c("return to owner", "rto-adopt") ~ "Returned to owner",
    outcome_type == "transfer"                          ~ "Transferred",
    outcome_type %in% c("euthanasia", "died")           ~ "Died or euthanized",
    TRUE                                                ~ "Other outcome"
  ))
```

### Features known at intake

The analysis only uses information the shelter has when an animal arrives, because the goal is to flag animals at the door.

```{r}
stays_clean <- stays_clean |>
  mutate(
    # Age: turn text like "2 years" or "3 weeks" into a number of days
    age_number = parse_number(age_upon_intake),
    age_days = case_when(
      str_detect(age_upon_intake, "year")  ~ age_number * 365,
      str_detect(age_upon_intake, "month") ~ age_number * 30,
      str_detect(age_upon_intake, "week")  ~ age_number * 7,
      str_detect(age_upon_intake, "day")   ~ age_number,
      TRUE                                 ~ NA_real_
    ),
    age_days = if_else(age_days < 0, NA_real_, age_days),

    # Sex and spay/neuter status, split out of one combined column
    sex = case_when(
      str_detect(sex_upon_intake, "Female") ~ "female",
      str_detect(sex_upon_intake, "Male")   ~ "male",
      TRUE                                  ~ "unknown"
    ),
    fixed = case_when(
      str_detect(sex_upon_intake, "Neutered|Spayed") ~ "fixed",
      str_detect(sex_upon_intake, "Intact")          ~ "intact",
      TRUE                                           ~ "unknown"
    ),

    # Did the animal arrive with its own name? (names starting with * were given by the shelter)
    has_own_name = !is.na(name) & !str_detect(name, fixed("*")),

    # When did it arrive?
    intake_year  = year(intake_date),
    intake_month = month(intake_date, label = TRUE),

    # Group the 20 arrival conditions into a handful of meaningful groups
    condition_group = case_when(
      intake_condition == "Normal"  ~ "Normal",
      intake_condition == "Injured" ~ "Injured",
      intake_condition %in% c("Sick", "Medical", "Med Attn", "Med Urgent",
                              "Neurologic", "Parvo", "Panleuk", "Congenital",
                              "Agonal")           ~ "Sick or medical",
      intake_condition %in% c("Neonatal", "Nursing") ~ "Neonatal or nursing",
      intake_condition %in% c("Behavior", "Feral")   ~ "Behavior or feral",
      intake_condition == "Aged"     ~ "Aged",
      intake_condition == "Pregnant" ~ "Pregnant",
      TRUE                           ~ "Other or unknown"
    ),
    condition_group = factor(condition_group,
                             levels = c("Normal", "Injured", "Sick or medical",
                                        "Neonatal or nursing", "Aged", "Pregnant",
                                        "Behavior or feral", "Other or unknown")),

    # Age groups, using the age in days from earlier
    age_group = cut(age_days,
                    breaks = c(-Inf, 56, 365, 365 * 5, Inf),
                    labels = c("Under 8 weeks", "8 weeks to 1 year",
                               "1 to 5 years", "Over 5 years"))
  )
```

### Decisions I made

| Decision | Why |
|---|---|
| Dogs and cats only | Wildlife, birds, and other species have very different outcomes |
| Each intake matched to the animal's next outcome | Animals can enter the shelter more than once |
| Animals with no recorded outcome kept as "still in shelter" as of 5 May 2025 | We know they waited at least that long (called "censoring") |
| Stays with no outcome that lasted over a year removed | Almost certainly missing records, not real stays |
| Owner-requested euthanasia and wildlife intakes removed | Those animals were never available for adoption |
| Died and euthanized grouped together | Both are non-live outcomes, and most deaths happened in the shelter's care |
| "rto-adopt" counted as returned to owner | An assumption: an owner reclaiming an animal |
| Only information known at intake used as predictors | The goal is to flag animals when they arrive |
| Models fit separately for dogs and cats, with repeat visits by the same animal grouped together | The two species behave differently, and one animal's stays are not independent of each other |

After these steps the analysis covers `r format(nrow(stays_clean), big.mark = ",")` stays: `r format(sum(stays_clean$animal_type == "Dog"), big.mark = ",")` dogs and `r format(sum(stays_clean$animal_type == "Cat"), big.mark = ",")` cats. Of these, `r format(sum(stays_clean$still_in_shelter), big.mark = ",")` had not yet left the shelter when the data ended.

## Exploring the data

### How stays end

Dogs and cats leave the shelter in different ways, which matters for any question about "time to adoption." An animal that is reclaimed by its owner or transferred to another organization can no longer be adopted from this shelter.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Source: Austin Animal Center, Oct 2013 to May 2025."

stays_clean |>
  filter(outcome_group != "Unknown outcome") |>
  count(animal_type, outcome_group) |>
  group_by(animal_type) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = share, y = reorder(outcome_group, share), fill = animal_type)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(share, accuracy = 1)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent,
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = species_colors) +
  labs(title = "How stays end for dogs and cats",
       subtitle = "Share of each species' stays",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

Roughly half of both species are adopted. Dogs are far more likely to be reclaimed by an owner, often within days, while cats are far more likely to be transferred to rescue partners and other shelters.

### Intakes over time

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "2013 and 2025 are left out because the data covers only part of those years. Source: Austin Animal Center."

stays_clean |>
  filter(intake_year %in% 2014:2024) |>
  count(intake_year, animal_type) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = intake_year, y = n, colour = animal_type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = species_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2014:2024) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(title = "Dog intakes fell much further than cat intakes after 2020",
       subtitle = "Dog and cat intakes per year, 2014 to 2024",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

Intakes of both species fell by roughly half in 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic. By 2024, cat intakes were about 12% below their 2014 to 2019 average, while dog intakes were still about half of theirs. Since 2023 the shelter has taken in more cats than dogs. The data cannot say why, but because the mix of animals changed, the analysis will check whether results differ across time periods.

### Condition on arrival

Animals arrive in very different states. Most are in normal condition, but a meaningful minority arrive injured, sick, or too young to eat on their own.

```{r}
#| echo: false

stays_clean |>
  count(condition_group, name = "stays") |>
  mutate(share = scales::percent(stays / sum(stays), accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Condition on arrival", "Stays", "Share of all stays"),
               align = c("l", "r", "r"),
               format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

### Who is most at risk?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Conditions with fewer than 1,000 stays for a species are not shown (see appendix). Source: Austin Animal Center."

stays_clean |>
  filter(outcome_group != "Unknown outcome") |>
  group_by(animal_type, condition_group) |>
  summarise(share = mean(outcome_group == "Died or euthanized"),
            stays = n(),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(stays >= 1000) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = share, y = reorder(condition_group, share), fill = animal_type)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent,
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = species_colors) +
  labs(title = "Injured and sick cats are most at risk",
       subtitle = "Share of stays ending in death or euthanasia, by condition on arrival",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

Injured and sick animals are far more likely to die or be euthanized than animals that arrive in normal condition, and the gap is much wider for cats: about 29% of injured cats and 22% of sick cats, compared with 12% and 11% of dogs. Animals that arrive in normal condition rarely have this outcome (2.3% of cats, 1.6% of dogs).

## Survival analysis

### How long until each outcome?

Each stay ends in one of several ways: adoption, return to owner, transfer, or death or euthanasia. The curves below show, for each day since arrival, the share of stays that have already ended in a given way. Stays still open when the data ended are counted as "censored," meaning we know they lasted at least that long.

```{r}
stays_cr <- stays_clean |>
  filter(outcome_group != "Unknown outcome") |>
  mutate(event = if_else(outcome_group == "Still in shelter",
                         "Censored", outcome_group),
         event = factor(event, levels = c("Censored", "Adopted",
                                          "Returned to owner", "Transferred",
                                          "Died or euthanized", "Other outcome")))

cm_species <- cuminc(Surv(los_days, event) ~ animal_type, data = stays_cr)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Stays still open when the data ended are treated as censored. Source: Austin Animal Center."

cm_species |>
  ggcuminc(outcome = "Adopted", theme = theme_get()) +
  scale_color_manual(values = species_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 180, 30)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 180)) +
  labs(title = "How quickly are dogs and cats adopted?",
       subtitle = "Share of stays ended in adoption by day since arrival",
       x = "Days since arrival", y = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

Dogs are adopted faster at first. Within a week, 22% of dog stays and 13% of cat stays have ended in adoption, and by day 30 the shares are 37% and 28%. The gap then closes: the cat curve keeps climbing while the dog curve flattens, and the two cross at roughly day 75. By day 90, 47% of cat stays and 46% of dog stays have ended in adoption. Past day 90 both curves flatten at close to half of all stays, with cats slightly ahead.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Share of stays that have ended in each outcome, by day since arrival. Source: Austin Animal Center."

cm_species |>
  ggcuminc(outcome = c("Adopted", "Returned to owner",
                       "Transferred", "Died or euthanized"),
           theme = theme_get()) +
  facet_wrap(~ outcome, ncol = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = species_colors) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = rep("solid", 4)) +
  guides(linetype = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 90, 30)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 90)) +
  labs(title = "How stays end over time",
       x = "Days since arrival", y = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

The other outcomes differ even more by species. About one in five dog stays (21%) ends with the dog going back to its owner within a week, compared with 3.5% of cats. Cats are far more likely to be transferred: 30% of cat stays end in a transfer within the first week, versus 14% of dog stays. Deaths and euthanasia are less common and happen mostly early: 4.0% of cat stays and 1.7% of dog stays within a week, rising only slightly by day 90.

These curves show shares of all arrivals, not the chance that an animal still waiting will be adopted. A dog reclaimed on day 1 never enters the adoption pool, so the models in the next section look at each outcome separately.

```{r}
#| echo: false

cm_species |>
  broom::tidy(times = c(7, 30, 60, 90)) |>
  filter(outcome != "Other outcome") |>
  select(outcome, strata, time, estimate) |>
  mutate(estimate = scales::percent(estimate, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = time, values_from = estimate, names_prefix = "Day ") |>
  arrange(outcome, strata) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Outcome", "Species", "By day 7", "By day 30",
                             "By day 60", "By day 90"),
               align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

### Does age at arrival matter?

```{r}
cm_age <- cuminc(
  Surv(los_days, event) ~ species_age,
  data = stays_cr |>
    filter(!is.na(age_group)) |>
    mutate(species_age = paste(animal_type, age_group, sep = " | "))
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Stays still open when the data ended are treated as censored. Source: Austin Animal Center."

cm_age |>
  broom::tidy(times = 1:90) |>
  filter(outcome == "Adopted") |>
  separate_wider_delim(strata, delim = " | ", names = c("species", "age_group")) |>
  mutate(age_group = factor(age_group, levels = levels(stays_clean$age_group))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = estimate, colour = age_group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ species) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.85) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 90, 30)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(title = "Animals 8 weeks to 1 year old are adopted fastest",
       subtitle = "Share of stays ended in adoption by day since arrival",
       x = "Days since arrival", y = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

cm_age |>
  broom::tidy(times = c(7, 30, 90)) |>
  filter(outcome == "Adopted") |>
  separate_wider_delim(strata, delim = " | ", names = c("species", "age_group")) |>
  mutate(age_group = factor(age_group, levels = levels(stays_clean$age_group)),
         estimate = scales::percent(estimate, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  select(species, age_group, time, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = time, values_from = estimate, names_prefix = "Day ") |>
  arrange(species, age_group) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Species", "Age at arrival",
                             "By day 7", "By day 30", "By day 90"),
               align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r"))
```

Age at arrival makes a large difference, but what it changes depends on the species. In both species, animals between 8 weeks and 1 year old are adopted fastest and most often: 56% of cats and 58% of dogs in that group are adopted within 90 days, and 25% of cats and 32% of dogs within the first week.

For dogs, older age mostly changes how stays end. The share adopted falls from 58% (8 weeks to 1 year) to 38% (1 to 5 years) and 24% (over 5 years), but the share returned to their owners rises from 17% to 32% to 46%. Almost half of dogs over 5 years old go home with their owners, so their low adoption share reflects reclaims as much as longer waits.

For cats, the two adult groups are adopted at similar rates (35% each), but the oldest cats are the most likely to die or be euthanized: 12% of cats over 5 years old, compared with 3% to 7% of younger cats.

The youngest animals differ by species. Puppies under 8 weeks are adopted quickly (22% within a week, 57% within 90 days). Kittens under 8 weeks start slowly (5% within a week) and reach 47% by day 90, and 43% of them are transferred to other organizations.

These are shares of all arrivals. Shares at day 90 do not add up to 100% because some stays ended in other ways or were still open.

```{r}
#| echo: false

cm_age |>
  broom::tidy(times = 90) |>
  filter(outcome != "Other outcome") |>
  separate_wider_delim(strata, delim = " | ", names = c("species", "age_group")) |>
  mutate(age_group = factor(age_group, levels = levels(stays_clean$age_group)),
         estimate = scales::percent(estimate, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  select(species, age_group, outcome, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = outcome, values_from = estimate) |>
  select(species, age_group, Adopted, `Returned to owner`,
         Transferred, `Died or euthanized`) |>
  arrange(species, age_group) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Species", "Age at arrival", "Adopted",
                             "Returned to owner", "Transferred",
                             "Died or euthanized"),
               align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

### Does condition on arrival matter?

```{r}
cm_cond <- cuminc(
  Surv(los_days, event) ~ species_cond,
  data = stays_cr |>
    filter(condition_group %in% c("Normal", "Injured", "Sick or medical",
                                  "Neonatal or nursing")) |>
    mutate(species_cond = paste(animal_type, condition_group, sep = " | "))
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Stays still open when the data ended are treated as censored. Source: Austin Animal Center."

cm_cond |>
  broom::tidy(times = 1:90) |>
  filter(outcome == "Adopted") |>
  separate_wider_delim(strata, delim = " | ", names = c("species", "condition")) |>
  mutate(condition = factor(condition, levels = levels(stays_clean$condition_group))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = estimate, colour = condition)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ species) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.85) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 90, 30)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(title = "Adoption by condition on arrival",
       subtitle = "Share of stays ended in adoption by day since arrival",
       x = "Days since arrival", y = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

cm_cond |>
  broom::tidy(times = 90) |>
  filter(outcome != "Other outcome") |>
  separate_wider_delim(strata, delim = " | ", names = c("species", "condition")) |>
  mutate(condition = factor(condition, levels = levels(stays_clean$condition_group)),
         estimate = scales::percent(estimate, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  select(species, condition, outcome, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = outcome, values_from = estimate) |>
  select(species, condition, Adopted, `Returned to owner`,
         Transferred, `Died or euthanized`) |>
  arrange(species, condition) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Species", "Condition on arrival", "Adopted",
                             "Returned to owner", "Transferred",
                             "Died or euthanized"),
               align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

Condition on arrival strongly affects where animals end up. Animals that arrive in normal condition are adopted most often: 52% of cats and 48% of dogs within 90 days. Among animals that arrive injured or sick, only about 27% of cats and 30% of dogs are adopted, and many do not leave alive: within 90 days, 29% of injured cats and 22% of sick cats died or were euthanized, compared with 12% and 11% of dogs.

Neonatal and nursing animals mostly leave by transfer to another organization (69% of cats and 53% of dogs). Adoption is very slow at first for these animals: only about 1% of neonatal cats are adopted in the first month. Neonatal dogs are adopted slowly until around day 55 to 60, when their curve rises sharply and ends above those of injured and sick dogs. The data cannot say why, but the timing is consistent with puppies reaching adoptable age at around eight weeks.

### Which factors matter most?

Age, condition, and intake type overlap: kittens often arrive as neonates, older animals often arrive sick, and strays can be reclaimed while surrendered animals mostly cannot. To separate them, I fit a Cox regression model for each outcome, separately for dogs and cats. Each model estimates how much a factor changes the rate of an outcome (a **hazard ratio**) while holding the other factors equal. For adoption, an animal that leaves another way, such as being reclaimed or transferred, stops being at risk of adoption. Repeat visits by the same animal are grouped together so that the uncertainty estimates are not too narrow.

The first chart below shows the average effect of each factor over the whole stay. Because the effects change during a stay, the section after it splits them by phase.

```{r}
stays_model <- stays_clean |>
  filter(outcome_group != "Unknown outcome", !is.na(age_group)) |>
  mutate(
    condition_model = case_when(
      condition_group %in% c("Normal", "Injured", "Sick or medical",
                             "Neonatal or nursing") ~ as.character(condition_group),
      TRUE ~ "Other"),
    condition_model = factor(condition_model,
                             levels = c("Normal", "Injured", "Sick or medical",
                                        "Neonatal or nursing", "Other")),
    age_group   = relevel(age_group, ref = "8 weeks to 1 year"),
    sex_fixed   = relevel(factor(paste(sex, fixed)), ref = "female intact"),
    intake_type = factor(intake_type,
                         levels = c("Stray", "Owner Surrender",
                                    "Public Assist", "Abandoned")),
    era = if_else(intake_year <= 2019, "2013 to 2019", "2020 to 2025")
  )

dogs <- stays_model |> filter(animal_type == "Dog")
cats <- stays_model |> filter(animal_type == "Cat")

# cluster(animal_id) groups repeat visits by the same animal together
fit_adopt_dog <- coxph(Surv(los_days, outcome_group == "Adopted") ~
                         age_group + condition_model + sex_fixed +
                         intake_type + has_own_name + era + cluster(animal_id),
                       data = dogs)
fit_adopt_cat <- coxph(Surv(los_days, outcome_group == "Adopted") ~
                         age_group + condition_model + sex_fixed +
                         intake_type + has_own_name + era + cluster(animal_id),
                       data = cats)
fit_death_dog <- coxph(Surv(los_days, outcome_group == "Died or euthanized") ~
                         age_group + condition_model + sex_fixed +
                         intake_type + has_own_name + era + cluster(animal_id),
                       data = dogs)
fit_death_cat <- coxph(Surv(los_days, outcome_group == "Died or euthanized") ~
                         age_group + condition_model + sex_fixed +
                         intake_type + has_own_name + era + cluster(animal_id),
                       data = cats)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

label_terms <- function(df) {
  df |>
    mutate(label = case_when(
      str_detect(term, "^age_group")       ~ paste("Age:", str_remove(term, "^age_group")),
      str_detect(term, "^condition_model") ~ paste("Condition:", str_remove(term, "^condition_model")),
      str_detect(term, "^sex_fixed")       ~ paste("Sex:", str_remove(term, "^sex_fixed")),
      str_detect(term, "^intake_type")     ~ paste("Intake:", str_remove(term, "^intake_type")),
      str_detect(term, "^has_own_name")    ~ "Arrived with a name",
      str_detect(term, "^era")             ~ paste("Period:", str_remove(term, "^era")),
      TRUE ~ term))
}

get_hr <- function(fit, species, outcome) {
  broom::tidy(fit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
    mutate(species = species, outcome = outcome)
}

hr_all <- bind_rows(
  get_hr(fit_adopt_dog, "Dog", "Adopted"),
  get_hr(fit_adopt_cat, "Cat", "Adopted"),
  get_hr(fit_death_dog, "Dog", "Died or euthanized"),
  get_hr(fit_death_cat, "Cat", "Died or euthanized")
) |>
  label_terms()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals. The dashed line at 1 means no difference from the reference group. Animals whose sex was not recorded (about 3.5% of stays) are not shown, because almost none were adopted. Source: Austin Animal Center."

hr_all |>
  filter(outcome == "Adopted", label != "Sex: unknown unknown") |>
  mutate(label = factor(label, levels = rev(unique(label)))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = label, colour = species)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), size = 0.35) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.2, 2)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = species_colors) +
  labs(title = "Average effect over the whole stay (read with caution)",
       subtitle = "Rate of adoption compared with the reference group (more than 1 = faster)",
       x = "Hazard ratio (log scale)", y = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

Each dot shows how much faster (to the right of the dashed line) or slower (to the left) animals in that group are adopted than the reference group, among animals still waiting and with the other factors in the model held equal. The reference groups are age 8 weeks to 1 year, normal condition, intact females, strays, arriving without a name, and arriving before 2020. A line that crosses the dashed line means the data cannot distinguish that group from its reference group.

Because these effects change during a stay (see the appendix), the next chart splits them by phase.

### Effects change over the stay

The check in the appendix shows that the effect of almost every factor changes during a stay, so one hazard ratio per factor hides the story. Below, the same model is fit separately for three phases of a stay: the first two weeks, weeks three to eight, and everything after eight weeks. Each phase only includes animals still waiting at its start.

```{r}
# The three phases of a stay (in days since arrival)
windows <- tibble(window = c("Days 0 to 14", "Days 15 to 56", "Day 57 onward"),
                  from   = c(0, 14, 56),
                  to     = c(14, 56, Inf))

# Fit the model for one phase, following only animals still waiting at its start
fit_window <- function(data, event_label, from, to) {
  data |>
    mutate(t = los_days + 0.5) |>   # half a day added so same-day outcomes can be used
    filter(t > from) |>
    mutate(tstart = from,
           tstop  = pmin(t, to),
           status = outcome_group == event_label & t <= to) |>
    coxph(Surv(tstart, tstop, status) ~ age_group + condition_model +
            sex_fixed + intake_type + has_own_name + era + cluster(animal_id),
          data = _)
}

# Fit every phase in a list of phases for one species and outcome, and collect the results
fit_windows <- function(data, species, event_label, win = windows) {
  pmap(win, function(window, from, to) {
    fit_window(data, event_label, from, to) |>
      broom::tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
      mutate(species = species, window = window)
  }) |>
    bind_rows()
}

hr_windows <- bind_rows(
  fit_windows(dogs, "Dog", "Adopted"),
  fit_windows(cats, "Cat", "Adopted")
) |>
  label_terms() |>
  mutate(window = factor(window, levels = windows$window))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Hazard ratios for adoption in three phases of a stay, with 95% confidence intervals. The dashed line at 1 means no difference from the reference group. Animals whose sex was not recorded (about 3.5% of stays) are not shown, because almost none were adopted. Source: Austin Animal Center."

hr_windows |>
  filter(label != "Sex: unknown unknown") |>
  mutate(label = factor(label, levels = rev(unique(label)))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = label, colour = species)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), size = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ window) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.03, 4)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = species_colors) +
  labs(title = "What speeds up or slows down adoption, by phase of the stay",
       subtitle = "Rate of adoption compared with the reference group (more than 1 = faster)",
       x = "Hazard ratio (log scale)", y = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

The effects of age and condition change during a stay, and in some cases reverse. Compared with animals 8 weeks to 1 year old, older animals are adopted more slowly in every phase, but the gap narrows. In the first two weeks, animals over 5 years old are adopted at about a quarter (cats) to a third (dogs) of the reference rate, and animals aged 1 to 5 years at about 40% to 50%. After eight weeks the rates are about 70% (over 5 years) and 80% to 85% (1 to 5 years) of the reference rate.

Animals under 8 weeks old at arrival follow a different pattern. In the first two weeks kittens are adopted at about a quarter of the reference rate and puppies at about three quarters. In weeks 3 to 8 kittens are still slower (about two thirds of the reference rate) while puppies are about 1.2 times as fast. Among animals still waiting after eight weeks, puppies are adopted about three times as fast as the reference group and kittens about 1.5 times as fast.

Injured animals are adopted at about 30% of the rate of animals in normal condition during the first two weeks, in both species. The gap narrows to about two thirds in weeks 3 to 8. After eight weeks injured dogs are adopted slightly faster than dogs in normal condition (1.13 times as fast), while injured cats are still about 15% slower. Sick or medical animals show a similar early gap (about half the normal rate for dogs and about a third for cats). For dogs it disappears after the first two weeks, but for cats it persists at about 80% of the normal rate.

Neonatal and nursing animals are barely adopted in the first two weeks (5% to 10% of the normal rate) and are adopted at about a third of the normal rate in weeks 3 to 8. After eight weeks, neonatal dogs still waiting are adopted about 1.6 times as fast as dogs in normal condition, while neonatal cats do not differ from normal. These estimates describe animals still waiting, so they leave out the many animals that were transferred or died earlier.

Animals that arrive with a name are adopted faster in every phase: about 1.3 to 1.7 times as fast in the first eight weeks and about 14% faster after that. Owner surrenders are adopted faster than strays in the first two weeks (about 1.4 times as fast for cats and 1.1 times for dogs) but not afterwards, and for dogs somewhat more slowly (about 10% to 15%). Public assist intakes are adopted far more slowly than strays in the first two weeks, especially dogs (13% of the stray rate for dogs, 35% for cats). Dogs stay about a third slower afterwards, while cats do not differ.

Sex and spay/neuter status have smaller effects. Compared with intact females, other groups of dogs are adopted up to about 20% more slowly. Cats are within about 15% in the first eight weeks, with spayed and neutered cats about 20% to 30% slower after that. Since 2020, cats have been adopted about 15% to 20% faster in every phase, while dogs were adopted about a third more slowly in the first two weeks and have not differed much since. These are associations, not proof of cause: for example, a name probably signals a pet that came from a home.

About 5,800 stays (3.5%) involve animals whose sex was not recorded at intake. These animals are almost never adopted: 1 of 5,028 cats and 24 of 744 dogs. Most were transferred to other organizations (85% of the cats and 64% of the dogs), and 11% of the cats and 14% of the dogs died or were euthanized. Most were under 8 weeks old at arrival (61% of the cats and 73% of the dogs). The data cannot say why sex is missing. These animals are left out of the charts above because their adoption rate cannot be estimated, and they do not affect the other adoption results.

### What raises the risk of death or euthanasia?

Deaths and euthanasia are rarer than adoptions and happen mostly early in a stay, so this model uses two phases: the first two weeks, and everything after. A ratio above 1 means a higher rate of death or euthanasia than the reference group, among animals still in the shelter. Euthanasia depends on shelter decisions as well as on the animal, and the data cannot say whether any of these outcomes could have been prevented.

```{r}
windows_death <- tibble(window = c("Days 0 to 14", "Day 15 onward"),
                        from   = c(0, 14),
                        to     = c(14, Inf))

hr_death_windows <- bind_rows(
  fit_windows(dogs, "Dog", "Died or euthanized", windows_death),
  fit_windows(cats, "Cat", "Died or euthanized", windows_death)
) |>
  label_terms() |>
  mutate(window = factor(window, levels = windows_death$window))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Hazard ratios for death or euthanasia in two phases of a stay, with 95% confidence intervals. The dashed line at 1 means no difference from the reference group. Source: Austin Animal Center."

hr_death_windows |>
  mutate(label = factor(label, levels = rev(unique(label)))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = label, colour = species)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), size = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ window) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.25, 1, 4, 16)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.05, 40)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = species_colors) +
  labs(title = "What raises the risk of death or euthanasia, by phase of the stay",
       subtitle = "Rate of death or euthanasia compared with the reference group (more than 1 = higher risk)",
       x = "Hazard ratio (log scale)", y = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

## Limitations

- **One shelter in one city.** Results may not apply to other shelters.
- **Ages are approximate.** The shelter records age as rounded whole units ("2 years," "3 weeks"), so `age_days` is an estimate.
- **Some outcomes may be missing.** Stays with no recorded outcome that are under a year old are treated as still in the shelter on 5 May 2025. Some may be missing records instead.
- **Matching assumes complete records.** If an intake or outcome is missing, an animal could be paired with the wrong visit.
- **Old and new files can't be linked.** The animal ID format changed in 2025, so the newer data is analyzed separately.
- **2020 was unusual.** COVID-19 changed intake patterns.
- **Some grouping choices are assumptions.** For example, "rto-adopt" is treated as return to owner, and died and euthanized are combined.
- **Only intake information is used.** Things that happen during a stay (behavior, medical treatment, marketing) are not in the data.
- **Reclaims and arrival type overlap.** Animals that arrive as strays can be claimed by their owners, but animals surrendered by an owner generally cannot, so intake type affects how stays end and has to be accounted for in the model.
- **Missing sex.** About 3.5% of stays have no recorded sex, and almost none of these animals were adopted. The reason is not recorded, so adoption results for these animals cannot be interpreted.
- **Model assumptions.** The proportional hazards check shows that the effect of almost every factor changes during a stay, so the main results are estimated separately for three phases of the stay (days 0 to 14, 15 to 56, and 57 onward). The single-model estimates are averages and should be read with that in mind. In the adoption models, animals that leave another way are treated as no longer available for adoption, so the results describe animals still waiting, not all arrivals.

### Model checks: events per group

Each group in a model needs enough events (adoptions or deaths) for its estimate to be stable. A rough rule is at least 10 to 20 events per group.

```{r}
stays_model |>
  group_by(animal_type, condition_model) |>
  summarise(stays = n(),
            adopted = sum(outcome_group == "Adopted"),
            died_euth = sum(outcome_group == "Died or euthanized"),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Species", "Condition (model groups)", "Stays",
                             "Adopted", "Died or euthanized"),
               format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

### Model checks: proportional hazards

The models assume each factor has the same effect throughout the stay. This check tests that and plots how each effect changes over time. With this many animals, the test flags even tiny departures, so the plots matter more than the p-values: a flat line means the effect is steady, and a sloping or curving line means it changes during the stay. The check uses the same models without the repeat-visit grouping, which affects only the confidence intervals and not how effects change over time.

Result: for cats, every factor except period fails the test, and for dogs every factor does. The plots show large changes in effect over the stay, so the main results are estimated separately for three phases of the stay.

```{r}
fit_zph_cat <- coxph(Surv(los_days, outcome_group == "Adopted") ~
                       age_group + condition_model + sex_fixed +
                       intake_type + has_own_name + era, data = cats)
fit_zph_dog <- coxph(Surv(los_days, outcome_group == "Adopted") ~
                       age_group + condition_model + sex_fixed +
                       intake_type + has_own_name + era, data = dogs)

zph_cat <- cox.zph(fit_zph_cat)
zph_dog <- cox.zph(fit_zph_dog)

zph_table <- function(z) {
  z$table |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    tibble::rownames_to_column("term") |>
    mutate(p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(digits = 1)
}
```

**Cats: adoption model**

```{r}
zph_table(zph_cat)
```

#| fig-cap: "How each factor's effect on adoption changes over the stay: age, condition, sex, intake type, arriving with a name, and period. A flat line would mean a steady effect. For factors with several levels, each panel combines the levels, so read the shape of the line, not the values."

par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (i in 1:6) plot(zph_cat, var = i, resid = FALSE)
```

```

par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
